title: What does OSHA 1910.1030 require for bloodborne pathogens training?
description: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 training rules: who needs it, the 14 required elements, annual timing, trainer and language rules, and 3-year records, at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, requires employers to train every employee with occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials. Training must be free, during working hours, given at initial assignment and at least annually within one year of the previous session, and repeated when tasks change exposure. It must cover 14 listed elements, include live questions and answers, and be recorded for 3 years.
keyTakeaways: Training is triggered by occupational exposure, defined as reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials from the employee's duties, not by job title.
Timing is at initial assignment, at least annually thereafter (within one year of the previous training), and whenever new or modified tasks affect exposure.
Paragraph (g)(2)(vii) lists 14 minimum elements, ending with an opportunity for interactive questions and answers with the person conducting the training.
Training records must show dates, content or summary, trainer names and qualifications, and attendee names and job titles, and be kept for 3 years.
Federal penalties proposed after January 15, 2025 reach $16,550 per serious violation and $165,514 per willful or repeated violation.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, and states with OSHA-approved State Plans)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Employers in general industry, including hospitals, clinics, dental and medical offices, laboratories, home health, long-term care and emergency services
Each employee with occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials, including part-time and temporary staff
Employees in HIV and HBV research laboratories and production facilities, who need additional initial training

sections.heading: Who must receive bloodborne pathogens training?

blocks.text: Every employee with occupational exposure must be trained. [29 CFR 1910.1030(b)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/section-1910.1030) defines occupational exposure as "reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane, or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials that may result from the performance of an employee's duties." Other potentially infectious materials include listed body fluids such as saliva in dental procedures, unfixed human tissue, and certain cell or tissue cultures.

The trigger is the task, not the title. A receptionist who never handles specimens may fall outside scope, while a housekeeper who removes regulated waste, a laundry worker handling contaminated linen, or a designated first aider may fall inside it. The employer's exposure determination, required as part of the exposure control plan, is the list that drives who is trained. For how this standard fits with other OSHA training duties, see [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements). This page states the position as at November 2026.

sections.heading: When is bloodborne pathogens training due, and how often?

blocks.text: Training is due at the time of initial assignment to tasks where occupational exposure may occur, and at least annually after that. The standard is precise about the annual cycle: paragraph (g)(2)(iv) says annual training "shall be provided within one year of their previous training," so a 13-month gap is a violation even if the employee was trained in each calendar year.

Additional training is required when modified or new tasks or procedures affect an employee's exposure, and it may be limited to the new exposures. Training must be provided at no cost to the employee and during working hours. For scheduling methods that avoid drift past the 12-month mark, see [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What must a bloodborne pathogens training program cover?

blocks.text: Paragraph (g)(2)(vii) sets 14 minimum elements. Several of them are specific to the employer, which is why a generic course alone rarely satisfies the standard. The table maps each element to its source and to the evidence that shows it was covered.

sections.heading: What does the standard say about trainers, language and online delivery?

blocks.text: The trainer must be knowledgeable in the subject matter as it relates to the specific workplace, and materials must be "appropriate in content and vocabulary to educational level, literacy, and language of employees." A workforce with limited English proficiency therefore needs materials and delivery it can understand.

The standard does not ban self-paced or online training, but element (N) requires "an opportunity for interactive questions and answers with the person conducting the training session." A module with no route to a knowledgeable person does not meet that text. Employers using online courses commonly add a live session, a scheduled call or a monitored channel, and record how employees used it.

Employees in HIV or HBV research laboratories and production facilities need more before working with those agents: demonstrated proficiency in standard microbiological practices, prior experience handling human pathogens or tissue cultures, and, for those without experience, a graded progression of tasks that excludes infectious agents until proficiency is shown.

sections.heading: What training records must be kept, and for how long?

blocks.text: Training records must include the dates of the sessions, the contents or a summary, the names and qualifications of the trainers, and the names and job titles of everyone who attended. Under paragraph (h)(2)(ii) they must be kept for 3 years from the date of training, and paragraph (h)(3) makes them available on request to employees, their representatives and OSHA.

Two related duties often surface in the same inspection. The exposure control plan must be reviewed and updated at least annually and when tasks or positions change, and employers must solicit input from non-managerial employees responsible for direct patient care in selecting safer sharps and document that solicitation. Employee medical records under the standard are kept for the duration of employment plus 30 years, which is a separate file from training records. For audit preparation, see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: What are the penalties, and do state plans change the rules?

blocks.text: Violations can bring civil penalties at the amounts in [29 CFR 1903.15(d)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1903/section-1903.15). For penalties proposed after January 15, 2025, a serious or other-than-serious violation can reach $16,550, and a willful or repeated violation up to $165,514 per violation, with a minimum of $11,823 for willful violations.

States with OSHA-approved State Plans, such as California, enforce their own occupational safety standards, including their own bloodborne pathogens standard, and their penalty amounts can differ. Employers in those states should check the state version as well as the federal text. No change to the federal standard was proposed in the Federal Register between January 2024 and November 2026 based on a search of OSHA documents mentioning bloodborne pathogens.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry separates the generic elements of the standard from the site-specific ones and links the site-specific elements to the current exposure control plan version, so a plan update flags which content and which employees need refreshing. See how this works for [healthcare and life sciences organizations](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: Does annual bloodborne pathogens training have to be repeated in full?
faqs.a: The standard does not define a shorter refresher. Annual training is part of the same training program, and the minimum elements in paragraph (g)(2)(vii) apply to that program, so annual sessions should still address all 14. Additional training required after a change in tasks may be limited to the new exposures, under paragraph (g)(2)(v).

faqs.q: Can a video or online course satisfy OSHA bloodborne pathogens training?
faqs.a: Only if the program also gives employees an opportunity for interactive questions and answers with the person conducting the training, as element (N) requires, and covers the site-specific elements such as the employer's exposure control plan and post-exposure procedure. A generic course with no access to a knowledgeable person does not meet the text.

faqs.q: Do employees who decline the hepatitis B vaccine still need training?
faqs.a: Yes. Training is required for every employee with occupational exposure. Information on the hepatitis B vaccine is one of the training elements, and employees who decline the vaccine must sign the mandatory declination statement in Appendix A to the standard.

faqs.q: Who can conduct bloodborne pathogens training?
faqs.a: Anyone knowledgeable in the subject matter covered by the training elements as it relates to the workplace being addressed. The standard does not require a specific certification, but the trainer's qualifications must be recorded in the training records under paragraph (h)(2)(i)(C).
